tips.title: Two ureters, one urethra
tips.body: A **ureter** runs from each kidney to the bladder, so there are **two**. The **urethra** carries urine out of the body, and there is **one**. Getting them the wrong way round is avoidable and common.

tips.title: The liver makes urea, the kidney removes it
tips.body: Excess **amino acids** cannot be stored, so the **liver** breaks them down into **urea**. The blood carries it to the **kidney**, which filters it out. Saying the kidney makes urea is a clear error.

tips.title: Too large to be filtered
tips.body: **Proteins and blood cells** stay in the blood because filtration works by **size**. That one phrase — *too large to be filtered* — answers a whole family of questions about what is and is not in the filtrate.

tips.title: Follow the ADH chain in order
tips.body: **ADH → permeability of the collecting duct → water reabsorbed → volume and concentration of urine.** Questions give you one end and ask for the other, so learn it as a chain and you can start from either.

tips.title: No urea, same glucose
tips.body: Dialysis fluid has **no urea**, so urea diffuses out down a steep gradient; and the **same glucose** as blood, so there is no gradient and none is lost. The fluid's composition is what does the work.

why.matters:
Cells sit in a watery solution and water crosses their membranes by **osmosis**, so the concentration of the blood is not a detail — too dilute and cells burst, too concentrated and they shrink. Something has to hold it steady whatever you drink.

The kidneys do that and dispose of **urea** at the same time. Their method is surprising: throw nearly everything out of the blood, then take back exactly what is wanted. It sounds wasteful and it is the reason the system works at all.

examples.title: Why the kidney throws out the glucose and then takes it back
examples.body:
Filtration in the kidney works by **size**. Small molecules are pushed out of the blood and large ones — proteins, blood cells — stay behind, and that is the only distinction it can make.

So glucose leaves too, along with the water, ions and urea. Sorting happens afterwards, in **reabsorption**: all the glucose is taken back, and as much water as the body needs. It is the same logic as tipping out a drawer to find one thing — crude, and far simpler than a filter that could recognise every molecule it met.

examples.title: Why your urine is darker in the morning
examples.body:
You have gone eight hours without drinking, so the blood is a little concentrated. The pituitary responds by releasing more **ADH**, which makes the **collecting duct** more permeable to water.

More water is therefore reabsorbed into the blood, and what is left is a small volume of concentrated, dark urine. Drink a litre of water and the opposite happens within the hour: less ADH, a less permeable duct, and a large volume of pale urine. The colour is a readout of a feedback loop.

visual.alt: A flow chart of the ADH response: blood that is too concentrated makes the pituitary release more ADH, the collecting duct becomes more permeable, more water is reabsorbed, and less and darker urine is produced

examples.title: What is in a bag of dialysis fluid, and why
examples.body:
Dialysis works entirely by **diffusion**, so every ingredient of the fluid is a decision about a concentration gradient.

It contains **no urea**, so urea diffuses out of the blood down a steep gradient and keeps going. It contains the **same glucose** as blood, so there is no gradient and none is lost. And it has the ion concentration of **healthy** blood, so a patient with too much of an ion loses the excess and stops there. Nothing is pumped: the recipe does the sorting.

steps.title: Why water content must be controlled
steps.body:
This whole topic is **Biology only** (7.10B and 7.18B to 7.22B). ADH (7.20B) is **Higher tier** only.

Cells sit in a watery solution, and water moves in and out of them by **osmosis** — from where it is more dilute to where it is more concentrated, through the partially permeable cell membrane.

That makes the concentration of the blood a matter of life and death for a cell:

- If the blood becomes **too dilute**, water moves **into** the cells. An animal cell has no cell wall, so it **swells and may burst**.
- If the blood becomes **too concentrated**, water moves **out** of the cells. They **shrink**, and the reactions inside them cannot work properly.

Keeping the water content of the blood constant is called **osmoregulation**, and it is done by the **kidneys**.

Water is gained by **drinking** and from **food**, and lost in **urine**, in **sweat**, in **breath** and in faeces. Of those, only the amount lost in **urine** can be adjusted — you cannot choose to sweat less on a hot day. So the kidney is the organ that makes the balance work.

One piece of vocabulary worth getting right: a **plant** cell has a **cell wall**, so it does not burst; it becomes turgid. This topic is about **animal** cells, which do.

steps.title: The urinary system
steps.body:
The **urinary system** has four parts, and the specification asks you to describe its structure.

- **Kidneys** — two of them. They **filter the blood** and make urine.
- **Ureters** — two tubes, one from each kidney, carrying urine to the bladder.
- **Bladder** — stores urine.
- **Urethra** — the single tube carrying urine out of the body.

Blood arrives at each kidney through the **renal artery** and leaves through the **renal vein**. *Renal* simply means *of the kidney*.

Two names are easy to swap, and the difference is worth fixing now: a **ureter** carries urine **from a kidney to the bladder**, and there are **two**; the **urethra** carries it **out of the body**, and there is **one**.

**Where the urea comes from.** The body cannot store excess **amino acids**. In the **liver**, the excess is broken down, and this produces **urea** — a toxic waste product which is carried in the blood to the kidneys and removed. So the liver makes urea and the kidney removes it, which is a distinction questions test directly.

steps.title: The nephron: filtration and reabsorption
steps.body:
Each kidney contains about a million tiny tubes called **nephrons**, and the whole of kidney function happens in them. The specification names three stages.

**The parts of a nephron, in the order the filtrate passes through them**, and how each part's structure suits its job:

- **Glomerulus** — a knot of capillaries. Blood arrives at **high pressure**, which forces small molecules out of it: this is **filtration**.
- **Bowman's capsule** — a cup wrapped round the glomerulus that **collects the filtrate**.
- **Convoluted tubule** — a long, coiled tubule where **all the glucose is reabsorbed** into the blood by **active transport**. Active transport needs energy from respiration, so the cells lining it have **many mitochondria**. Its length gives plenty of time and surface for reabsorption.
- **Loop of Henle** — a hairpin loop where more **water and ions** are reabsorbed.
- **Collecting duct** — where the last of the water that the body needs is **reabsorbed**. How permeable it is to water is what ADH controls. What is left drains to the ureter as **urine**.

steps.title: ADH and the collecting duct
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)* The amount of **water** reabsorbed is adjusted by a hormone: **ADH**, antidiuretic hormone, released by the **pituitary gland**.

ADH acts on the **collecting duct** of the nephron, and what it changes is the duct's **permeability to water**:

**If the blood is too concentrated** (you have sweated, or not drunk enough):

- **more ADH** is released
- the collecting duct becomes **more permeable** to water
- **more water is reabsorbed** into the blood
- the result is a **small volume of concentrated urine**

**If the blood is too dilute** (you have drunk a lot):

- **less ADH** is released
- the collecting duct becomes **less permeable**
- **less water is reabsorbed**
- the result is a **large volume of dilute urine**

The chain is always the same four links: **ADH → permeability → water reabsorbed → volume and concentration of urine**. Questions give you one end and ask for the other, so learning it as a chain rather than as two lists means you can start from either end.

And this is **negative feedback** once more: the response opposes the change. Blood too concentrated leads to water being kept, which dilutes it back.

steps.title: When the kidneys fail
steps.body:
If the kidneys stop working, **urea and excess water and ions build up** in the blood. Urea is toxic, and the change in water and ion balance damages cells. Kidney failure is fatal if untreated. There are two treatments.

**Kidney dialysis.** A machine does the kidney's job. Blood is taken from the body and flows on one side of a **partially permeable membrane**; **dialysis fluid** flows on the other.

The dialysis fluid is made to contain:

- the **same concentration of glucose and ions** as healthy blood, so **none of those is lost** — there is no concentration difference for them to diffuse down
- **no urea**, so urea **diffuses out** of the blood down a steep concentration gradient

That design is the clever part, and it is regularly examined: the fluid's composition decides what is removed and what is kept.

Dialysis must be repeated regularly — typically several sessions a week, each of several hours — and the diet must be controlled between sessions.

**A kidney transplant.** A kidney from a donor is placed in the body. It works continuously, so there are no dialysis sessions and no dietary restriction, though immunosuppressant drugs must be taken for life.

But the recipient's **immune system may reject** the donor kidney as foreign. To reduce the risk, the kidney is **tissue matched**: the donor, often a close relative, is chosen so that the antigens on their cells are as similar as possible to the recipient's, and the kidney is less likely to be recognised as foreign. Even so, **immunosuppressant drugs** must be taken for life, which leave the patient more vulnerable to infection. And donor kidneys are **in short supply**, so there is a waiting list.

steps.title: Going deeper: why filter first and take it back?
steps.body:
**The obvious question.** Filtering out glucose and then reabsorbing all of it looks wasteful. Why not leave it in the blood to begin with?

Because **filtration cannot select**. It works by **size**: blood is pushed at high pressure through a membrane, and anything small enough goes through. Urea is small, so it passes — but so do water, glucose and ions, because they are small too. There is no way to filter out urea alone.

So the kidney uses a two-stage design: **filter indiscriminately by size, then take back selectively what is useful.** That is exactly what **selective reabsorption** means, and the word *selective* is the contrast with the unselective filtration before it.

This also explains **why glucose in the urine is a sign of diabetes**. Normally all the filtered glucose is reabsorbed. If the blood glucose concentration is very high, more glucose is filtered than the nephron can take back, and the excess appears in the urine. The kidney has not failed; it has been overwhelmed.

**Evaluating the two treatments.** A question asking you to compare dialysis and transplant wants both sides and a judgement:

- **Dialysis** is available to everyone who needs it and carries no rejection risk, but it is **time consuming**, restricts the **diet**, and must continue indefinitely.
- **A transplant** restores normal life and needs no dialysis sessions, but donor kidneys are **scarce**, surgery carries risk, the kidney **may be rejected**, and **immunosuppressants** leave the patient vulnerable to infection.

A sensible judgement: a transplant is generally better **when a matching kidney is available**, and dialysis is what keeps a patient alive **until** one is — which is closer to how the two are actually used than declaring either superior.

**Three points of precision.**

- **Two ureters, one urethra.** Swapping them is common and avoidable.
- **The liver makes urea; the kidney removes it.** Saying the kidney makes urea is a clear error.
- **ADH changes permeability**, not the amount of filtering. The kidney filters the same volume; what changes is how much water is **taken back**.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Water moves in and out of cells by **osmosis**. Blood **too dilute** makes an animal cell **burst**; **too concentrated** makes it **shrink**.
- **Osmoregulation** is control of the water content of the blood, done by the **kidneys**.
- The urinary system: **kidneys → ureters → bladder → urethra**. Two ureters, one urethra.
- **Urea** is made in the **liver**, from the breakdown of **excess amino acids**, and removed by the kidneys.
- Each kidney contains about a million **nephrons**.
- **Filtration**: blood at high pressure in the **glomerulus** and **Bowman's capsule**. **Water, glucose, ions and urea** are filtered out.
- **Proteins and blood cells are too large** to be filtered.
- **Selective reabsorption**: **all the glucose** is taken back, because it is useful.
- **Most of the water** is reabsorbed, the exact amount adjusted according to need; what is left becomes **urine**.
- **ADH** from the **pituitary** changes the **permeability of the collecting duct** to water.
- Blood **too concentrated** → **more ADH** → more permeable → **more water reabsorbed** → a **small volume of concentrated urine**.
- Blood **too dilute** → **less ADH** → less water reabsorbed → a **large volume of dilute urine**.
- **Dialysis**: the fluid has **no urea** so urea diffuses out, and the **same glucose** as blood so none is lost.
- **Transplant**: no dialysis sessions, but immunosuppressants are taken for life; donors are scarce, and even a **tissue-matched** kidney may be **rejected**.

questions.prompt: Describe how a nephron filters the blood and forms urine, naming the structures involved and explaining what happens to glucose, water and urea.
questions.solution: Blood arrives at the nephron under high pressure in a knot of capillaries called the glomerulus, which sits inside a structure called the Bowman's capsule. The high pressure forces small molecules out of the blood and into the capsule. These include water, glucose, ions and urea. Proteins and blood cells are not filtered out because they are too large to pass through, so they remain in the blood. The liquid that has been filtered then passes along the nephron, where selective reabsorption takes place. All of the glucose is reabsorbed back into the blood in the convoluted tubule, by active transport, because glucose is useful to the body and none should be wasted. Most of the water is also reabsorbed, and the exact amount depends on how much water the body needs at the time. Urea is not reabsorbed, because it is a toxic waste product that must be removed. What remains at the end, which is the urea together with the excess water and excess ions, passes out of the nephron as urine.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Filtration.** Blood arrives at **high pressure** in the **glomerulus**, a knot of capillaries inside the **Bowman's capsule**. The pressure forces **small molecules** out into the capsule: **water, glucose, ions and urea**.

**Proteins and blood cells** are **too large** to be filtered, so they stay in the blood. That is what makes it filtration — it separates by **size**.

**Selective reabsorption.**

- **All the glucose** is reabsorbed into the blood, in the **convoluted tubule** by **active transport**, because it is useful and none should be wasted. The cells there have many mitochondria to supply the energy.
- **Most of the water** is reabsorbed; the exact amount depends on what the body needs.
- **Urea is not reabsorbed** — it is toxic waste that must be removed.

**What is left.** Urea, together with the excess water and excess ions, passes on as **urine**.

The word **selective** is the contrast with the filtration before it: filtering cannot choose, so the nephron filters everything small and then takes back what it wants.

questions.prompt: Compare kidney dialysis with a kidney transplant as treatments for kidney failure, and explain how the composition of dialysis fluid allows it to clean the blood.
questions.solution: In kidney dialysis, blood from the patient is passed through a machine where it flows on one side of a partially permeable membrane, with dialysis fluid flowing on the other side. The dialysis fluid contains no urea at all, so there is a steep concentration gradient and urea diffuses out of the blood and into the fluid. The fluid contains the same concentration of glucose as normal blood, so there is no concentration gradient for glucose and none of it is lost from the blood. It also contains ions at the concentration found in healthy blood, so that any excess ions are removed while normal levels are maintained. Dialysis is available to everyone who needs it and there is no risk of rejection, but it must be repeated several times a week for several hours at a time, and the patient's diet has to be controlled between sessions. A kidney transplant gives the patient a donor kidney which works continuously, so no dialysis sessions are needed and the diet can be normal. However, donor kidneys are in short supply, the surgery carries risks, and the patient's immune system may reject the donated kidney, so the kidney is tissue matched and immunosuppressant drugs must be taken for life, which leave the patient more vulnerable to infection. On balance a transplant is generally preferable when a suitable kidney is available, while dialysis keeps a patient alive until one can be found.

questions.modelAnswer:
**How dialysis works.** Blood flows on one side of a **partially permeable membrane**; **dialysis fluid** flows on the other. What the fluid contains decides what is removed:

- **No urea** → a steep **concentration gradient**, so urea **diffuses out** of the blood.
- **The same glucose concentration as blood** → **no gradient**, so **no glucose is lost**.
- **Ions at healthy blood levels** → excess ions are removed while normal levels are kept.

**Dialysis.**

- *For:* available to everyone who needs it; no rejection risk.
- *Against:* several sessions a week of several hours each; the diet must be controlled; it continues indefinitely.

**Transplant.**

- *For:* the kidney works continuously, so normal life and a normal diet.
- *Against:* donor kidneys are **scarce**; surgery carries risk; even a **tissue-matched** kidney may be **rejected**, so **immunosuppressants** are needed for life, raising the risk of infection.

**Judgement.** A transplant is generally preferable **when a suitable kidney is available**; dialysis is what keeps a patient alive **until** one is found. That is closer to how the two are actually used than declaring either simply better.

questions.prompt: The cells lining the convoluted tubule of a nephron contain many mitochondria. What is the best explanation?
questions.solution: Glucose is reabsorbed **against** its concentration gradient by **active transport**, which needs **energy from respiration**; mitochondria supply it. Filtration happens in the glomerulus, urea is made in the liver, and osmosis needs no energy.

markScheme.description: active transport of glucose needs energy from respiration

options: They filter the blood at high pressure
Glucose is reabsorbed by active transport, which needs energy
They make urea from excess amino acids
Water is reabsorbed by osmosis, which needs a lot of cellular energy

questions.prompt: Put these parts of the urinary system in the order that urine passes through them, starting where it is made.
questions.solution: Urine is made in the **kidney**, carried by a **ureter** to the **bladder**, stored there, and leaves the body through the **urethra**.

markScheme.description: kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra

questions.prompt: Which blood vessel carries blood that has been filtered away from a kidney?
questions.solution: **The renal vein.** Blood arrives at each kidney through the renal artery, is filtered in the nephrons, and the cleaned blood leaves through the renal vein, which carries it back towards the heart. *Renal* means *of the kidney*. The ureter is not a blood vessel: it carries urine from the kidney to the bladder, and the urethra carries urine out of the body.

markScheme.description: the renal vein

options: The renal vein
The renal artery
The ureter
The urethra

questions.prompt: A person loses a great deal of water by sweating and does not drink, so their blood becomes more concentrated than normal. What happens to their red blood cells?
questions.solution: **Water leaves and the cells shrink.** Water moves by osmosis from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated one through the partially permeable cell membrane. If the blood plasma is more concentrated than the cytoplasm, water moves out of the red blood cells, and they shrink, so the reactions inside them cannot work properly. Cells swell and may burst in the opposite case, when the blood is too dilute; osmosis is the movement of water, not of salt; and animal cells have no cell wall, which is why they can burst or shrink at all. Keeping the water content of the blood constant, osmoregulation, is what protects them.

markScheme.description: water leaves the cells by osmosis and they shrink

options: Water enters the cells by osmosis and they may burst
Water leaves the cells by osmosis and they shrink
The cells take in salt by osmosis and become larger
Nothing changes, because the cell wall keeps their shape

questions.prompt: A test shows glucose in a patient's urine. Further tests show that the patient's kidneys are healthy. Which statement is the best explanation?
questions.skill: selective reabsorption and glucose in urine
questions.solution: **The nephron has been overwhelmed, not damaged.** Glucose is small enough to be filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus, and normally **all** of it is reabsorbed into the blood in the convoluted tubule by **active transport**. Active transport has a limit: there are only so many carrier proteins. If the blood glucose concentration is very high, as in untreated diabetes, more glucose is filtered than the tubule can take back, and the excess passes on into the urine. The kidney has not failed; it has been given more than it can reabsorb. Glucose does not reach the bladder except through the nephron, and the liver makes urea from excess amino acids, not glucose.

markScheme.description: blood glucose is so high that more is filtered than the tubule can reabsorb by active transport

options: The patient's kidneys have stopped filtering glucose out of the blood, so it collects in the bladder instead of in the nephron
The patient's blood glucose is so high that more glucose is filtered than the tubule can reabsorb by active transport
The patient has eaten a large meal, and the glucose from it passes straight from the gut into the bladder without entering the blood
The patient's liver has turned excess amino acids into glucose rather than urea, and the kidney cannot filter this type of glucose

questions.prompt: A student writes: 'When the blood is too concentrated, ADH makes the kidney filter less water out of the blood.' What is wrong with this statement?
questions.skill: what ADH does and does not change
questions.solution: **ADH changes permeability, not filtration.** The kidney filters the same volume of fluid from the blood whatever its water content; the filtrate contains water, glucose, ions and urea. What ADH alters is how much of the filtered water is **taken back**. When the blood is too concentrated the pituitary gland releases more ADH, the **collecting duct** becomes more permeable to water, more water is reabsorbed into the blood, and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced. Water is never stored in the bladder for later use, the glomerulus is not where ADH acts, and insulin controls blood glucose, not water.

markScheme.description: ADH does not change filtration; it makes the collecting duct more permeable so more filtered water is reabsorbed

options: ADH makes the kidney filter more water, not less, so that the extra water can be stored in the bladder until it is needed
Nothing is wrong: ADH narrows the vessels of the glomerulus so that less water is filtered out when the blood is concentrated
The hormone involved is insulin, not ADH, and it acts on the liver to release water from glycogen when the blood is concentrated
ADH does not change filtration; it makes the collecting duct more permeable, so more of the filtered water is reabsorbed

questions.prompt: Name the cup-shaped part of a nephron that surrounds the glomerulus and collects the fluid filtered out of the blood.
questions.solution: **Bowman's capsule.** Blood arrives in the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries, at high pressure, which forces water, glucose, ions and urea out through the capillary walls. Bowman's capsule is the cup wrapped round the glomerulus that collects this filtrate and passes it into the convoluted tubule, where all the glucose is reabsorbed. Proteins and blood cells are too large to pass through, so they stay in the blood.

markScheme.description: Bowman's capsule

questions.prompt: In one day, a person's kidneys filter 150 litres of fluid out of the blood into the nephrons. In the same day the person produces 1.5 litres of urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is reabsorbed back into the blood.
questions.solution: Reabsorbed $= 150 - 1.5 = 148.5$ litres. Percentage $= \dfrac{148.5}{150} \times 100 = 99\%$. Only 1% of what is filtered leaves as urine. The kidney filters indiscriminately by size and then selectively reabsorbs almost all of the water, along with all of the glucose, so that the urea is removed without the useful substances being lost.

markScheme.description: subtracts the urine from the filtered volume, 148.5 litres, and divides by 150 (× 100)

questions.prompt: At rest, a person produces urine at a rate of 60 cm³ per hour. After drinking a litre of water, the person produces 540 cm³ of urine over the next 90 minutes. Calculate how many times greater the rate of urine production is after the drink than at rest.
questions.solution: Put both rates in the same units. At rest: 60 cm³ per hour $= \dfrac{60}{60} = 1$ cm³ per minute. After the drink: $\dfrac{540}{90} = 6$ cm³ per minute. So the rate is $\dfrac{6}{1} = 6$ times greater. (In cm³ per hour: 90 minutes is 1.5 hours, $540 \div 1.5 = 360$, and $360 \div 60 = 6$.) The drink made the blood more dilute, so the pituitary gland released **less ADH**, the collecting duct became **less permeable** to water, **less water was reabsorbed**, and a large volume of dilute urine was produced.

markScheme.description: converts both rates to the same units: 1 and 6 cm³ per minute, or 60 and 360 cm³ per hour
divides one rate by the other

questions.prompt: A patient with kidney failure receives a kidney from a donor. Explain why the patient's immune system may reject the new kidney, and describe two precautions taken to reduce the risk of rejection.
questions.solution: The cells of the donor kidney carry **antigens** that differ from the patient's own, so the patient's immune system recognises the kidney as **foreign** and attacks it. Two precautions reduce the risk. The kidney is **tissue matched**: a donor, often a close relative, is chosen whose antigens are as similar as possible to the patient's, so the kidney is less likely to be recognised as foreign. And the patient takes **immunosuppressant drugs** for life, which reduce the immune response, though they leave the patient more vulnerable to infection.

tissue matching (or blood-group matching): a donor, often a close relative, is chosen whose antigens are as similar as possible to the patient's

questions.modelAnswer: The immune system attacks anything it recognises as foreign. The cells of the donor kidney carry antigens on their surface that are different from the antigens on the patient's own cells, so the patient's white blood cells may recognise the kidney as foreign and attack it, which is rejection. Two precautions reduce the risk. First, the kidney is tissue matched: a donor is chosen, often a close relative, whose antigens are as similar as possible to the patient's, so the kidney is less likely to be recognised as foreign. Second, the patient takes immunosuppressant drugs for the rest of their life. These reduce the activity of the immune system so that it is less likely to attack the kidney, although they also leave the patient more vulnerable to infection.

questions.prompt: All of the glucose filtered into a nephron is reabsorbed into the blood in the convoluted tubule. Explain why this reabsorption has to use active transport rather than diffusion alone.
questions.solution: Glucose is **useful**: it is the substrate for respiration, so the body wants **all** of it back. Diffusion only moves a substance **down** its concentration gradient. The filtrate starts with glucose at the **same concentration** as the blood, so there is no gradient to drive diffusion at all, and diffusion could at best make the two concentrations equal, never empty the filtrate, so some glucose would be lost in the urine. **Active transport** moves glucose **against** its concentration gradient, from the dilute filtrate into the more concentrated blood, using energy from respiration, which is why the cells lining the tubule contain many mitochondria.

questions.modelAnswer: Filtration in the glomerulus works by size, so glucose, which is a small molecule, is forced out of the blood along with water, ions and urea. Glucose is the substrate for respiration and the body cannot afford to lose it, so all of it has to be returned to the blood. Diffusion cannot do this on its own. Diffusion moves a substance from where it is more concentrated to where it is less concentrated. The filtrate starts with glucose at the same concentration as the blood, so there is no concentration gradient and no net diffusion into the blood at all. Diffusion could at best make the two concentrations equal; it could never empty the filtrate, because as soon as any glucose was taken back the filtrate would be more dilute than the blood, and the remaining glucose would be lost in the urine. Active transport moves glucose against its concentration gradient, from the dilute filtrate into the more concentrated blood. It needs energy, which comes from respiration, and that is why the cells lining the convoluted tubule contain many mitochondria. The same reasoning explains why glucose appears in the urine when blood glucose is very high: the carrier proteins can only work so fast, and the excess passes on.

questions.prompt: A runner completes a marathon on a hot day, sweating heavily and drinking very little. Explain how the runner's body responds to keep the water content of the blood constant, and explain why this control matters to the runner's cells.
questions.solution: Sweating removes water, so the blood becomes **more concentrated**. This is detected, and the **pituitary gland** releases **more ADH** into the blood. ADH acts on the **collecting duct** of the nephron and makes it **more permeable** to water, so **more water is reabsorbed** from the filtrate into the blood, and the runner produces a **small volume of concentrated urine**. The water content of the blood rises back to normal and ADH release falls: the response opposes the change, which is **negative feedback**. It matters because water crosses cell membranes by **osmosis**. If the blood were too concentrated, water would leave the cells and they would **shrink**, so the reactions inside them could not work; if it were too dilute, water would enter and the cells, having no cell wall, would **swell and burst**.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that the blood becomes more concentrated or that less urine is produced, or that cells are affected by osmosis, with little linking of the steps

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes most of the ADH chain, more ADH so more water reabsorbed and concentrated urine, or explains the effect on cells by osmosis, but misses a link, such as the permeability of the collecting duct, or gives only one of the two parts

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a full chain: sweating makes the blood more concentrated, the pituitary releases more ADH, the collecting duct becomes more permeable, more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is produced, and the water content returns to normal by negative feedback; and explains that too concentrated blood would make cells lose water by osmosis and shrink, while too dilute blood would make them swell and burst

Says that this is detected and the pituitary gland releases more ADH into the blood
Explains that ADH makes the collecting duct of the nephron more permeable to water
Explains that more water is reabsorbed from the filtrate into the blood, so a small volume of concentrated urine is produced
Says that the water content of the blood returns to normal and ADH release falls: the response opposes the change, which is negative feedback

Explains why it matters: if the blood is too concentrated water leaves the cells by osmosis and they shrink, and if it is too dilute water enters and they swell and may burst, because animal cells have no cell wall

questions.modelAnswer:
**The disturbance.** Sweating loses a great deal of water, and the runner is replacing very little of it, so the water content of the blood falls and the blood becomes **more concentrated** than normal. The body cannot choose to sweat less on a hot day; the only loss it can adjust is the water leaving in urine, so the kidneys have to do the correcting.

**The response.** The change in the blood is detected by the brain, and the **pituitary gland** releases **more ADH** into the blood. ADH travels to the kidneys and acts on the **collecting duct** of each nephron, making it **more permeable** to water. As the filtrate passes down the collecting duct, **more water is reabsorbed** from it into the blood. The result is a **small volume of concentrated urine**: the urea is still removed, but far less water goes with it. The kidney filters the same volume as before; what has changed is how much of the filtered water is taken back.

**Negative feedback.** As water is kept in the blood, and once the runner drinks, the water content rises back towards normal. The pituitary then releases less ADH, the collecting duct becomes less permeable, and more water passes out in the urine. The response **opposes the change** and switches itself off when the change has been corrected, which is what negative feedback means, and it works in the other direction too: after a large drink, less ADH is released and a large volume of dilute urine is produced.

**Why it matters.** Cells sit in the watery plasma, and water crosses their partially permeable membranes by **osmosis**, from the more dilute side to the more concentrated side. If the blood were allowed to become too concentrated, water would leave the cells, they would **shrink**, and the reactions inside them would stop working properly. If it became too dilute, water would move into the cells; an animal cell has **no cell wall** to hold it, so it would **swell and burst**. Osmoregulation holds the blood's concentration steady so that neither happens, whatever the runner sweats or drinks.

examTechnique.body:
Name the structures: glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, collecting duct. A description that says the kidney filters the blood without naming where loses marks.

Say that proteins and blood cells are too large to be filtered, rather than that they are not filtered.

For glucose, say that all of it is reabsorbed and that this is selective reabsorption.

For ADH, work through the chain in order and include the permeability step, which is the one most often skipped.

For dialysis, explain the composition of the fluid in terms of concentration gradients rather than describing the machine.

When comparing dialysis with a transplant, give both sides and finish with a judgement.
examinerErrors: Saying the kidney produces urea rather than removing it.
Swapping the ureter and the urethra.
Saying proteins are reabsorbed rather than never filtered.
Saying some glucose is reabsorbed, when all of it is.
Saying ADH changes how much blood is filtered rather than the permeability of the collecting duct.
Getting the ADH direction backwards: more ADH gives concentrated urine, not dilute.
Explaining dialysis without mentioning concentration gradients.
Saying a transplant has no disadvantages.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer explains the two-stage design rather than reciting it: filtration cannot select because it works by size, so the nephron filters everything small and then takes back what is useful. That single insight explains selective reabsorption, why glucose appears in the urine in untreated diabetes, and why dialysis fluid must be made up so carefully. It follows the ADH chain through the permeability step every time. And in the evaluation it notices that dialysis and transplant are not really rivals — one sustains a patient until the other becomes possible.
